passage.text: In the woods near his house, Zach searched for stones to skip across the creek. Finally, he spotted the perfect skipping stone. It was flat and triangle-shaped. He crouched by the water, aimed, and let the stone fly. Yes! It whizzed halfway across the creek, bouncing against the water, and then it skimmed to the opposite side. The rock landed in a pile of leaves, next to some kind of orange object. Zach squinted. What was that?
There was only one way to find out.

Zach ran across the footbridge. When he finally reached the orange object, it turned out to be the most beautiful turtle Zach had ever seen. As he got closer to it, he saw that its shell contained other colors, such as brown, yellow, red. But mostly it was a warm, bright orange. Zach remembered reading that some box turtles were orange, but he had never seen one before. He felt really lucky.
"I think I should call you Sunset," Zach told the turtle.

Gently, Zach carried Sunset home and put him in an empty aquarium. He gave him a plastic bowl of water, but Sunset didn't drink. Zach offered him berries, but Sunset's head never left his shell. Instead, he sat as still as a stone.
"You'll get used to it here," Zach said. "Don't worry."

The next morning, Sunset finally poked his head out, just a little. Now Zach could see his red eyes, which looked sad. Sunset's shell seemed duller, too. It looked less like a sunset and more like a rusty old fence.

Zach and Sunset stared at each other through the glass. Zach thought about how Sunset must feel. In the woods, Sunset could go wherever he wanted. He could feel the sun on his orange shell and listen to the creek.
With a sigh, Zach placed Sunset in a shoebox and carried him to the woods. He walked to the exact spot where he had found him. Then he opened the shoebox to release the turtle.
"I'll still visit you," he whispered.

Then something caught his eye. It was the triangle stone, right where he had left it. He picked it up and bounced it across the creek. Triple skip! Zach turned to grin at Sunset, but he was surprised by what he saw. Sunset had stretched his head all the way out of his shell! His red eyes, lively now, gazed right into Zach's brown ones. It almost looked like he was grinning back.

passage.text: Anna, Greg, and Ethan sat around the table. Anna was reading from a paper that explained the rules of the robot contest for their science class. Anna, Greg, and Ethan had been sick when teams were picked. So although all the other students had been allowed to choose their teams, Mrs. Talent had put the three of them together.

They had named their team the Ruling Robots. So far, that was the only thing the three of them could agree on. Anna started reading the rules again while Greg tapped his fingers on the table and Ethan looked up at the ceiling.
"Okay, so the robot has to be fast, and it has to pick things up," said Anna.
"As I said before," Ethan started, "let's put together a robot arm, wheels, and a motor. The arm should be tall so that it can easily pick things up."

"But it has to go around corners quickly," Greg said. "A tall robot might fall over when it goes around corners. We need to make it like a race car, small and long and close to the ground, so it's fast."
Ethan rolled his eyes. "That idea is absurd," he said. "There's no way a robot like that would be able to pick anything up!"
Greg crossed his arms and frowned.
"How about a disk shape?" Anna offered. "Its base would be wide enough to support a tall arm, and it could still go around corners quickly. It's a bit of both ideas."
Greg and Ethan sat up and looked at each other. They said together, "That's perfect!"

With only two weeks to complete their task, the Ruling Robots got to work. They worked on their robot every day after school. They took turns bringing music and snacks for each meeting. The time they spent together seemed to fly by.

Finally, it was the day of the contest. The Ruling Robots watched the other teams' robots run through the course. One team had built a tall robot, which fell over when it zoomed around a corner. Another team had created a robot that looked like a race car, but its arm wasn't tall enough to pick up one of the objects. Anna looked at her teammates and smiled.

Then it was their turn. They steered their robot through the course and made it lift different objects with its arm. The robot stayed upright and finished the course with the best time. The Ruling Robots won the contest!
When Mrs. Talent asked them who came up with the winning design, the boys looked at Anna. Anna looked back at them and smiled. "We all did," Anna said. "None of us could have done it alone!"

They had named their team the Ruling Robots. So far, that was the only thing the three of them could agree on. Anna started reading the rules again while Greg tapped his fingers on the table and Ethan looked up at the ceiling.
"Okay, so the robot has to be fast, and it has to pick things up," said Anna.
"As I said before," Ethan started, "let's put together a robot arm, wheels, and a motor. The arm should be tall so that it can easily pick things up."

"But it has to go around corners quickly," Greg said. "A tall robot might fall over when it goes around corners. We need to make it like a race car, small and long and close to the ground, so it's fast."
Ethan rolled his eyes. "That idea is absurd," he said. "There's no way a robot like that would be able to pick anything up!"
Greg crossed his arms and frowned.
"How about a disk shape?" Anna offered. "Its base would be wide enough to support a tall arm, and it could still go around corners quickly. It's a bit of both ideas."
Greg and Ethan sat up and looked at each other. They said together, "That's perfect!"

With only two weeks to complete their task, the Ruling Robots got to work. They worked on their robot every day after school. They took turns bringing music and snacks for each meeting. The time they spent together seemed to fly by.

Finally, it was the day of the contest. The Ruling Robots watched the other teams' robots run through the course. One team had built a tall robot, which fell over when it zoomed around a corner. Another team had created a robot that looked like a race car, but its arm wasn't tall enough to pick up one of the objects. Anna looked at her teammates and smiled.

Then it was their turn. They steered their robot through the course and made it lift different objects with its arm. The robot stayed upright and finished the course with the best time. The Ruling Robots won the contest!
When Mrs. Talent asked them who came up with the winning design, the boys looked at Anna. Anna looked back at them and smiled. "We all did," Anna said. "None of us could have done it alone!"

title.text: The Day the Lights Went Out

passage.text: On a steamy, hot summer day, Nura and her dad found a place to cool off at the city's natural history museum. They were enjoying the dim green undersea room when suddenly the lights blinked off and on. With a final pop, the lights went out completely, leaving the room cloaked in black.
"Dad, what's going on?" Nura called out loudly with a frown on her face.
"I'm not sure, but we'll wait a minute and see if the lights come back on," Dad said calmly. In a moment, the glow of a flashlight approached. A museum worker waved the flashlight at them.
"There's a power outage across the city, so we have to close the museum," she said. "I'll walk you to the exit."

Nura and her dad stopped at Jasper's, their favorite shop, for ice cream. "What a day, huh?" Jasper greeted them, placing a cool towel on his pink forehead. "My freezers are out, so come on quick and get your cones." Nura and her dad ordered two cones, but when Nura's dad tried to pay, the owner waved his hand.
"Forget about it," he said. "It will all be soup soon, anyway!"

After a long, hot walk, Nura and her dad arrived home to find some of their neighbors on the steps outside their apartment building. Everyone looked sweaty, but they were talking and laughing together about the sizzling heat. They were sharing pitchers of ice water.
"I couldn't stand it in my apartment," Mrs. Fong said, fanning herself with a newspaper. "At least out here there's a little breeze."
Another neighbor shrugged. Nura recognized him as the man who lived in the apartment above hers.

A woman who lived downstairs was leaning against the doorway. "And I just stocked my refrigerator," she said. "If the power doesn't come on soon, the food will go bad and I'll have to throw it all away."

"I have some meat in the freezer, too," said Nura's dad. "Maybe I'll use the grill on the roof tonight. It would be nice to cook everything before it spoils. And it's been a while since I've hosted a cookout."
The woman in the doorway nodded. "I'll see what I have to contribute," she said. "I'll make sure to bring enough for everyone."
That evening, Nura and her neighbors gathered on the roof. Nura learned that the man from upstairs was named Sergey. The downstairs woman was Rachel.
As they finished their dinner, night fell over the city. For the first time in Nura's life, their street became completely dark.
She gazed up and gasped. Stars blinked overhead, thousands of bright dots in the black sky. She'd never seen such a sight.

The night air was thick and hot, but Nura didn't mind anymore. She had enjoyed free ice cream, and she had shared a rooftop dinner with her neighbors. She smiled to herself and continued to watch the stars.

title.text: The Day the Lights Went Out

passage.text: On a steamy, hot summer day, Nura and her dad found a place to cool off at the city's natural history museum. They were enjoying the dim green undersea room when suddenly the lights blinked off and on. With a final pop, the lights went out completely, leaving the room cloaked in black.
"Dad, what's going on?" Nura called out loudly with a frown on her face.
"I'm not sure, but we'll wait a minute and see if the lights come back on," Dad said calmly. In a moment, the glow of a flashlight approached. A museum worker waved the flashlight at them.
"There's a power outage across the city, so we have to close the museum," she said. "I'll walk you to the exit."

Nura and her dad stopped at Jasper's, their favorite shop, for ice cream. "What a day, huh?" Jasper greeted them, placing a cool towel on his pink forehead. "My freezers are out, so come on quick and get your cones." Nura and her dad ordered two cones, but when Nura's dad tried to pay, the owner waved his hand.
"Forget about it," he said. "It will all be soup soon, anyway!"

After a long, hot walk, Nura and her dad arrived home to find some of their neighbors on the steps outside their apartment building. Everyone looked sweaty, but they were talking and laughing together about the sizzling heat. They were sharing pitchers of ice water.
"I couldn't stand it in my apartment," Mrs. Fong said, fanning herself with a newspaper. "At least out here there's a little breeze."
Another neighbor shrugged. Nura recognized him as the man who lived in the apartment above hers.

A woman who lived downstairs was leaning against the doorway. "And I just stocked my refrigerator," she said. "If the power doesn't come on soon, the food will go bad and I'll have to throw it all away."

"I have some meat in the freezer, too," said Nura's dad. "Maybe I'll use the grill on the roof tonight. It would be nice to cook everything before it spoils. And it's been a while since I've hosted a cookout."
The woman in the doorway nodded. "I'll see what I have to contribute," she said. "I'll make sure to bring enough for everyone."
That evening, Nura and her neighbors gathered on the roof. Nura learned that the man from upstairs was named Sergey. The downstairs woman was Rachel.
As they finished their dinner, night fell over the city. For the first time in Nura's life, their street became completely dark.
She gazed up and gasped. Stars blinked overhead, thousands of bright dots in the black sky. She'd never seen such a sight.

The night air was thick and hot, but Nura didn't mind anymore. She had enjoyed free ice cream, and she had shared a rooftop dinner with her neighbors. She smiled to herself and continued to watch the stars.

Her gaze landed on her favorite hoodie, which she'd been looking for the day before. "That's where you went! I guess I shouldn't have waited so long to do the laundry," she whispered to herself. The hoodie was sticking out of a pile of dirty clothes on the floor. Ella grabbed the heap and dumped it into the laundry basket. It was a start, at least.

One book was about origami, the art of folding paper to make animals and other shapes. She had received it as a gift, with some pretty origami paper, but she'd never actually folded any of the paper. passage.text: As soon as Amanda read the invitation, she started jumping up and down. She could hardly believe her favorite cooking show had invited her to try out! Her hands shook as she dialed the number for her best friend, Joanna.

"This is so awesome, you just can't imagine!" Amanda shouted. "I got an invitation to try out for Kids Cook! I need to send in a cooking video, so can you please help me record it? Please, please?" Joanna was thrilled, and she agreed to record the video at Amanda's house the next day.
When Joanna arrived with her camera, Amanda was setting up in her kitchen.
"Are you making my favorite cheese and vegetable stew?" Joanna asked.

"No, it's my special spicy pasta dish, Pasta Amanda! Let's get started with the video. We'll need to record three different parts. Part one is my introduction, part two is the cooking demonstration, and in part three, we show the completed dish on a beautiful plate. Here—read my introduction."

Joanna grinned as she read through what Amanda had written. "This will be extraordinary, Amanda," Joanna said with a thumbs-up. Joanna set up the camera, and when she was ready to record, she shouted, "Action!" But at the sight of Joanna's camera, Amanda forgot what she was supposed to say. No words came out, and she looked ready to cry.
"No problem. Don't worry, we'll start over," said Joanna. "Just take a deep breath, forget about the camera, and pretend you're talking to me."
Amanda closed her eyes, breathed, and began again. This time she remembered what to say, and she spoke with a sparkling smile.
"Way to go!" Joanna exclaimed. She kept the camera going as Amanda chopped vegetables and stirred the spicy sauce.

When Amanda finished, she stopped to watch the video. "I forgot to mention the hot pepper," she said. "I also dropped that garlic on the stove. It can't look messy, so we'll have to redo the whole segment."
"Really?" Joanna asked, feeling tired and hungry. But she helped Amanda clean the stove and then recorded more chopping and stirring. Amanda's sauce smelled spicy and delicious.
This time when Amanda watched the video, she grinned.
"Wonderful. Let's eat now," said Joanna.
Amanda shook her head. "First, I need to create a perfect plate for the last part of the video."
Amanda prepared four separate plates, sprinkling herbs and olive oil over each. Joanna shook her head while she watched Amanda. Joanna's stomach growled as she glanced at the clock.
"Let's show this one," Amanda finally said, pointing to the last plate. Joanna, looking happy to be almost done, recorded Amanda with the finished dish.
"It's a wrap!" Amanda said at last. "You're the best, Joanna."
"It was no big deal! But can we have lunch now?" Joanna asked.
"Yes, and you can have the perfect plate," said Amanda.

"Jane's mother says she will have to stay home for two weeks," Mom explained. "So I'd like you two to bring Jane her homework and spend some time visiting her every day."

Santiago and Sofía were twins, and they were in Jane's class. Jane lived nearby, but they didn't think they had anything in common with her. All they knew was that Jane liked Frog City, a cartoon show the twins used to watch a few years ago. Now they were definitely too old for that cartoon.
After school the next day, Santiago and Sofía walked to Jane's house with her homework. Sofía also carried a small plant that their mother had bought for Jane.
"I don't know what to say to her, and I hope she doesn't want to discuss Frog City," Sofía sighed. Santiago just shook his head and shrugged.
Jane's mother greeted them at the door and led them to Jane's bedroom. Jane was sitting up in bed, with her leg in a cast on a pile of pillows. "Thanks," she said, taking the homework and the plant.
"No problem," Santiago said, shuffling his feet and looking around.
"Does your leg hurt?" Sofía asked, trying to think of an interesting topic of conversation.
"Not if I don't move, but sitting still all day is pretty boring," said Jane.
"Well, I guess you can watch Frog City, right?" Santiago said.
"I'm too old for that," Jane replied. "Lately, I've been reading the Star Team series."
"Oh, Star Team is sensational!" Santiago shouted. "I'm already on book five."
"I finished book three this morning, and I can't wait to start the next one!" Jane replied.
"I just read the fourth one, so you can borrow my copy!" Sofía offered.
The next day, the twins brought the book along with Jane's homework, and on Saturday, they visited again to talk about the series.
"I'm going to dress up as Lina from Star Team this Halloween," Jane said.
"We could go trick-or-treating together as Star Team!" Sofía added.
"Yes, I'll be Jinx, and Sofía can be Millie," said Santiago.

header.text: An adjective is a word that tells about a noun. Adjectives often tell what kind or how many.

sentences.text: Jodie saw three stars in the sky.
The adjective tells how many stars Jodie saw.

header.text: An adverb is a word that tells about a verb. Adverbs often tell how, when, or where.

sentences.text: Grace ran quickly.
The adverb tells how Grace ran.

contents.text: Most adverbs that tell how end in -ly, like the adverb quickly.

header.text: You can't always use -ly to tell whether a word is an adjective or an adverb, though.

sentences.text: She arrives soon.
Soon is an adverb that doesn't end in -ly.
Fred has a friendly dog.
Friendly is an adjective that ends in -ly.
